claim_grade: Mechanism (tax authority/land authority divergence): B-claim, qualitative case-study inference from 32 interviews plus documents, peer-reviewed (Tier 1 by venue). content_summary.point: Concept: tax authority/land authority divergence = public institutions hold formal legal/administrative power to tax property while authority to 'define, allocate, legitimate, or disclose land rights' remains partly in customary or informal institutions. Tax authority covers defining the base, assessing liability, billing, collecting, enforcing; land authority covers allocating land, validating rights, controlling or disclosing land information, influencing transactions.
content_summary.locator: Section 'Tax authority/land authority divergence: definition, dimensions, and scope conditions'; also Introduction para 4
content_summary.grep: Tax authority/land authority divergence refers to situations in which public institutions possess formal legal and administrative powers to tax property

content_summary.point: Who rates: Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs) 'have authority to mobilise local revenue through rates, rents, fees, fines, and licences, including property rates' under the Local Governance Act 2016.
content_summary.locator: Findings, 'Formal tax authority, the property rating base, and weak fiscal reach', para 1
content_summary.grep: Under the Local Governance Act 2016, MMDAs have authority to mobilise local revenue

content_summary.point: The base: general rates on premises are payable by the owner and levied on rateable value; rateable premises comprise buildings, structures or similar developments; rateable value is defined by the replacement cost of the buildings/structures after depreciation. So the main recurrent base is 'anchored to buildings, structures, and structural development rather than the unimproved value of land'.
content_summary.locator: Findings, same subsection, para 2
content_summary.grep: The rateable value is defined by reference to the replacement cost of the buildings

content_summary.point: Customary role in allocation: land 'held through stools, skins, families, and other landholding groups', chiefs as custodians or trustees; they retain influence over allocation, local recognition of rights and legitimacy of transactions.
content_summary.locator: Findings, 'Historical reproduction of land sensitivity and the rating settlement', para 1; Methodology, 'Case selection', para 2

content_summary.point: Land/site value as base: article defines LVT narrowly as 'a recurrent tax on the unimproved value of land, excluding buildings and improvements' (cites George 1879); says raising building rates 'would still focus the recurrent local tax on structures and improvements rather than on the site value created through urban growth, infrastructure provision, planning decisions'; leaves undeveloped land and speculative holding 'only weakly captured'. Compares full LVT, split-rate, vacant/underdeveloped land tax and betterment charges as 'not institutionally equivalent' but each needing reliable land information, defensible valuation, identifiable liability and legitimacy.

Not an argument for or against LVT; no empirical test of an LVT.

Insertion points: (1) people/andy-burnham.md, section '## Land Value Tax: From 2010 to the 2026 Campaign': a new paragraph after the paragraph that begins 'On 24 September 2026 the Resolution Foundation...' and before '## Winning the Leadership and Becoming Prime Minister'; also, in the paragraph ending 'no legislation had been published as of 6 September 2026.' (the sentence 'As of 11 August 2026 the reform is confirmed not to be in the 28 October 2026 Budget'), append that the Budget as delivered on 28 October 2026 contained no council-tax replacement or land/property-value tax measure (grep of the Red Book, speech, news story and costings for 'land value tax' and 'proportional property' returns nothing). (2) places/united-kingdom.md, section '## The 2026 LVT Moment: Andy Burnham's Premiership': one sentence after '...per the wiki's one-home-per-finding rule.' stating that the 28 October 2026 Budget, delivered by Chancellor John Healey, carried no LVT but confirmed the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (England, £2m+, from April 2028) and raised property-income tax rates; details on the Burnham page. Keep to the Treasury facts: A-claims from primaries. IMPORTANT CORRECTIONS to the brief's premises: (a) the £2m surcharge (HVCTS) is NOT new at this Budget: it was announced at Budget 2025 (gov.uk announcement dated 28 Nov 2025; Starmer government) and Budget 2026 confirmed its design (deferral, discounts and exemptions, premium); frame it as 'confirmed', never as announced by Burnham's government. (b) The 'doubling for homes empty 12 months' is a '100% premium' within the HVCTS, a surcharge on properties left 'substantially unfurnished and unoccupied for... 12 months or more'; the Budget documents contain no change to the ordinary council-tax empty-homes premium (grep 'empty' in the Red Book returns only a business-rates sentence). Use the sources' words, '100% premium', not 'doubling'. (c) The council takeover power is not a Budget measure and not new: it is an MHCLG press release of 27 Sept 2026 reforming existing Empty Dwelling Management Orders (EDMOs: councils may take over management of long-term empty homes for up to seven years, ownership staying with the owner); the qualifying empty period is cut from two years to six months and evidential requirements are removed. No legislative vehicle, commencement date or named minister is stated in the release; it does not mention the Budget. Present it separately as a 27 September announcement. (d) Property income rates rise by 2 percentage points a second time (Budget 2025 did the first), not a single new rate. Also optional: concepts/speculative-vacancy.md could take one sentence on the HVCTS 100% empty-property premium and the EDMO change (England) if T1 wants a vacancy-policy home; it currently has no England empty-homes policy content.
claim_grade: A-claims (official fact: what the government announced, rates, dates, thresholds, costings as the Treasury states them). Source Tier 1 (HM Treasury, HMRC, MHCLG, gov.uk). Revenue and household-count figures are the government's own estimates (official forecasts, not independently tested): B-claims if used as effects; use 'the government estimates'. No interpretive claim about Georgist significance is supported by the sources: the HVCTS is a banded charge on property value (land plus building) on a 2026 valuation, not a land value tax; the Treasury documents never use the term. Do not state it is 'the first step' toward LVT.

EDMOs allow councils to take over the management of long-term empty homes and return them to occupation for up to seven years while ownership remains with the property owner. uncertainties: Naming: gov.uk uses 'Budget 2026'; the gov.uk page titled 'What the Autumn Budget 2026 means for your energy bills' and the queue use 'Autumn Budget 2026'. Cite as 'Budget 2026 (28 October 2026)'.

The HVCTS tax information and impact note contains a typo, 'The government published its response to the consultation on 28 October 2028'; the Summary of Responses and fact sheet date it to Budget 2026 (28 October 2026). Do not repeat 2028.
Valuation body: 2025 announcement says 'Valuation Office Agency'; 2026 notes say 'Valuation Office (VO)' / 'HMRC VO'. Use 'Valuation Office' with the source, or avoid the acronym.

The Budget 2025 original HVCTS costing is in a separate Budget 2025 document not fetched; the combined exchequer table in the 2026 note merges both. 'About £400 million a year' comes from the fact sheet.

'Doubling' is the T0 task's wording; the sources say '100% premium'. Whether this means exactly twice the surcharge is not stated in the saved text (the premium base is not spelled out); T1 should not write 'doubles'. The Red Book and speech contain no ordinary council-tax empty-property change.

The EDMO release names no minister, legislative vehicle or start date, was published a month before the Budget, and is not in the Budget documents: do not attribute it to the Budget. EDMOs pre-existing is inferred from the press release's wording ('reforms to', 'reduce the period'), not from a statute fetched here.

Which Chancellor announced HVCTS at Budget 2025 is not stated in any saved file (the gov.uk pages say 'Budget 2025' only); the wiki's Muellbauer page says 'Starmer government'. Do not name that Chancellor.
The speech text on gov.uk has '[REDACTED POLITICAL CONTENT]' placeholders (as published); quotations should avoid those passages.

Red Book is signed 'James Murray' (HM Treasury, 28 October 2026); the HVCTS Summary of Responses foreword is signed by James Murray MP as Financial Secretary to the Treasury and Jim McMahon OBE MP, Minister for Local Government; these are as printed.
